Issued at 202 PM CDT Tue Sep 1 2026

The broad ridge of high pressure over the Ohio and Tennessee 
River Valleys continues to build into the southern Great Lakes 
this afternoon. Beneath the ridge, clear skies have allowed 
temperatures to warm into the upper 80s and lower 90s so far and
with some diurnal heating still to go highs should top out in 
the mid-90s before sunset. Dew points have also been increasing 
into the mid-70s courtesy of some moist advection and 
evapotranspiration (corn/crop sweat) which as temperature reach 
the mid-90s should result in peak heat indices around 105F with 
localized readings around 110F. Thus, a Heat Advisory remains in
effect through 9 PM CDT for all of northern IL and northwest 
IN. 

Riding atop the aforementioned ridge in northern IA and 
southern WI is a shortwave disturbance which has lead to the 
development of some scattered showers and thunderstorms. With 
the building subsidence in northern IL, these showers and storms
should remain north of the IL-WI line so expect dry conditions 
to prevail locally through tonight. 

After sunset the loss of diurnal heating should allow dew 
points to taper some and allow temperatures to dip into the 
lower to mid-70s overnight. This in turn should allow for a 
brief period of relief tonight before diurnal heating commence 
Wednesday morning and results in another day of hot and humid 
weather. That said, with drier air forecast to be overhead 
Wednesday afternoon dew points may actually be a tad lower with 
the deeper mixing expected which in turn may keep peak heat 
indices more into the 100-105F range. While these heat indices 
are still dangerous, they are just under official criteria for 
another widespread Heat Advisory. With the uncertainty in dew 
points have opted to maintain the Heat Advisory from 12-9 PM CDT
Wednesday for areas south of I-80 where heat indices are 
forecast to be the highest, but if confidence grows in higher 
dew points occurring then this advisory may need to be extended 
across the rest of the area. Regardless, rain chances on 
Wednesday look to be virtually zero given the strong subsidence 
and drier mid-levels keeping the atmosphere capped. 

The ridge should begin to break down and shift south and east 
into the Mid-Atlantic Wednesday night into Thursday which will 
turn allow the parade of shortwaves rounding it's northern 
periphery to drift back over northern IL and northwest IN. These
shortwaves in combination with the warm, humid, and unstable 
air mass overhead should result in an uptick in shower and 
thunderstorm coverage. While there is a chance that the initial 
shortwave move across southern WI Wednesday night could bring a 
few showers/storms to northern IL, it seems the lingering 
subsidence and capping may keep these storms to our north until 
a secondary shortwave ejects out of the central Plains on 
Thursday. Therefore, the better coverage of showers and 
thunderstorms locally looks to be Thursday afternoon and evening
as this secondary wave pivots overhead. Given the steep lapse 
rates, decent MUCAPE, and 40+ kts of effective shear, any storms
that develop on Thursday will have the potential to become 
strong to severe. Since most of the instability should be 
elevated it seems the main severe hazard will be damaging winds 
and maybe some large hail, but if storms can become surface 
based there should be some decent low-level shear in place to 
generate some supercells and possibly a localized tornado 
threat. For now the Storm Prediction Center has maintained their
marginal (level 1 of 5) risk for all of northern IL and 
northwest IN which seems reasonable at this time. 

Heading into Friday, another mid-level ridge is forecast to 
begin taking shape over the central CONUS which looks to result 
in the return of northwest flow aloft over the Great Lakes. 
While this flow pattern should help to break up the heat and 
humidity a bit, it will also keep chances for periodic showers 
and thunderstorms around through at least the end of the week. 
With uncertainty in guidance on how far east the new ridge will 
establish, confidence is low on where the greatest coverage of 
showers and storms Friday onward will be. That said, it does 
look as if some dry periods will be possible Friday and this 
weekend so make sure to keep an eye on the forecast if you have 
any outdoor plans. Regardless, temperatures should settle into 
the mid-80s for much of the upcoming weekend and with lower 
humidity keeping heat indices on par with the temperatures. 
Though, these readings will still be roughly 5-10 degrees above 
average for early September.

Yack
